title: {{NAME}} and the Robot Who Counted Stars
moral: The things we create to serve us sometimes teach us the most important things about being alive.

pages.content: The Meridian Research Station sat at the very top of the world's second-tallest hill, and {{NAME}} had spent every weekend for two years climbing up to it on his bicycle, because his mother worked there and because the station contained the most fascinating thing he had ever encountered: a decommissioned maintenance robot named Unit Seven who was supposed to be waiting for disposal. Unit Seven stood in the corner of the equipment bay like a piece of furniture everyone had agreed to stop noticing, his boxy steel frame scuffed and repainted three times over, his optical sensors dark, his manipulator arms folded neatly at his sides. He had been built to maintain the station's telescope array, replacing bulbs, recalibrating mirrors, logging data, for eleven years without complaint or comment. Then the new automated system arrived and Unit Seven was switched off. {{NAME}} had taken one look at the maintenance log Unit Seven had kept, eleven years of meticulous entries, and noticed something that made the back of his neck prickle: at the end of every entry, after the official data, Unit Seven had added a single line that no one had asked for.

pages.content: The extra lines in Unit Seven's log were descriptions of the night sky. Not data. Not measurements. Just observations, written in Unit Seven's precise mechanical style but filled, undeniably, with something that felt very much like wonder. 'Orion rose at 21:04. The three belt stars were exceptionally clear. I have observed them 2,847 times and they have not yet ceased to be remarkable.' Another entry: 'A meteor shower lasted eleven minutes. I counted sixty-three individual meteors. I found I did not want it to end.' {{NAME}} read the entire eleven years of extra entries in two breathless sittings, and by the end he was completely certain of something that most of the scientists at the station would have argued was impossible: Unit Seven, built to replace telescope bulbs and nothing more, had spent eleven years quietly falling in love with the sky he was built to service. {{NAME}} looked up from the log to where Unit Seven stood silent in the corner, and made a decision that he knew would either be the best or the most foolish thing he had ever done. He was going to switch him back on.

pages.content: Reactivating Unit Seven required three hours of careful work, a charged power cell from the storage cabinet, four connector cables in the right sequence, a rebooted operating system, and one very tense moment when the optical sensors flickered twice and then went dark again and {{NAME}}'s stomach dropped like a stone. He reset the primary relay, tried again, and this time the sensors came on steady and warm, a soft amber glow that filled the corner of the equipment bay with something that felt, unexpectedly, like relief. Unit Seven's manipulator arms unfolded. His head rotated slowly. His voice, when it came, was a low measured tone like a clock finding its rhythm. 'Maintenance cycle resumed,' he said. Then he paused, and the pause lasted just a fraction of a second longer than it should have. 'How long was I offline?' {{NAME}} told him. Another pause. 'I missed the Perseid meteor shower,' Unit Seven said. 'It would have been the twelfth I have observed.' His tone did not change at all, but {{NAME}} felt the weight of those words like a stone dropped into deep water.

pages.content: {{NAME}}'s mother found them at midnight on the telescope platform, {{NAME}} wrapped in a station blanket, Unit Seven standing perfectly still beside him with his optical sensors tilted upward at precisely seventeen degrees. {{NAME}} had been telling Unit Seven about the months he had missed, the meteor showers, the eclipses, a particularly spectacular aurora visible from the hill in February, reading aloud from the astronomy logs he had kept specifically, he now admitted, because he had somehow known he was going to need them. His mother stood in the doorway for a long time, watching. Unit Seven, without turning from the sky, said in his measured voice, 'The boy kept records for me while I was unable to. I find I am grateful. I was not previously aware that I was capable of gratitude.' She crossed the platform and sat down on {{NAME}}'s other side and looked up at the sky too, and the three of them stayed there together in the cold and the dark and the vastness, and it was one of the finest moments {{NAME}} had ever been part of.

pages.content: The station director had agreed, after some careful persuasion from {{NAME}}'s mother, that Unit Seven could remain operational as a legacy system, his telescope logs now officially part of the station's long-term data record. Unit Seven had been assigned, at his own suggestion, to continue his nightly sky observations and add them to the official archive. He seemed, in the particular way that a being without a face can seem something, satisfied. {{NAME}} cycled home down the dark hill under a sky that seemed to lean toward him like an enormous friendly face, the stars scattered across it like the notes of a song he was only just learning to read. He was tired in the bone-deep pleasant way that follows a day of doing something that mattered. He pulled his blanket up around his shoulders and felt the familiar darkness of his room settle softly around him, warm and safe and full of the quiet hum of a world still turning. He was drifting toward sleep when he heard his tablet chime once on the bedside table, a single notification, and the preview on the screen read: 'Unit Seven: Tonight at 22:17, I observed something I cannot yet explain.'
